reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Cleaning & EDA
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 12, Cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis. In the previous module, we learned how to build more advanced Pandas workflows. Now we are going to use those tools for one of the most important parts of analytics: deciding whether the data is trustworthy enough to analyze.

Cleaning is not simply deleting rows that look unusual. It means understanding the quality of the data, correcting problems when we have a good reason, and documenting what we changed.

[tts-break]

After cleaning, we move into exploratory data analysis, or EDA. EDA helps us understand what is in the dataset before we make stronger conclusions. We look at missing values, duplicate records, data types, categories, unusual values, and basic patterns.

Throughout this module, keep asking two questions: what problem do I see in the data, and what evidence supports the cleaning decision I am making?

slides.title: From advanced Pandas to Cleaning & EDA
slides.transcript:
Module 11 gave us the Pandas tools we need to transform, group, reshape, and validate tables. In this module, we use those tools for a more practical purpose: improving data quality and understanding the dataset before formal analysis.

Think of the process as a sequence. First, we inspect the data. Then we identify problems. Next, we make careful cleaning decisions. Finally, we explore the cleaned data to understand distributions and group differences.

[tts-break]

The important point is that cleaning and EDA are connected. If categories are inconsistent, your group summaries may be wrong. If duplicate rows remain, your totals may be inflated. If numeric values are stored as text, calculations may fail or produce misleading results.

This module also prepares us for Module 13, where we will use statistics and visualization on data that we have already inspected and cleaned.

slides.title: Our messy working dataset
slides.transcript:
For this module, we will intentionally work with a small messy dataset. It contains several realistic problems that you may see in real projects.

There is a duplicated order, missing values, an invalid date, inconsistent capitalization and spacing, a numeric column stored as text, and a few values that look suspicious.

The goal is not to fix everything immediately.

[tts-break]

Before we change anything, we should understand what is wrong. That is an important habit in professional analytics. If you start editing values too quickly, you may remove evidence that helps explain how the problem happened.

For example, a value of eleven hundred may be a data-entry error, but it may also be a legitimate large order. A missing region may need to stay missing if we do not have enough information to recover it.

As we work through the module, we will use the same dataset so you can see exactly how each cleaning step changes it.

slides.title: Start with a data audit
slides.transcript:
A data audit is the first systematic look at an unfamiliar dataset. Before we clean, we want to understand the structure.

Start with the shape to see how many rows and columns you have. Check the data types. Look at a few rows. Count missing values. For categorical columns, inspect the unique values or value counts.

[tts-break]

Run the code and look carefully at what Pandas reports. Do not focus only on whether the code runs. Ask what each output tells you.

For example, if amount is stored as an object instead of a numeric type, that is a clue that the column may contain text or inconsistent values. If the region column contains North, north, and north with spaces, those may represent the same category but appear as different groups.

A good audit gives you a list of issues to investigate before you start changing the data.

slides.title: Missing values: count and percentage
slides.transcript:
When we find missing values, the first step is to measure the problem.

A count tells us how many values are missing in each column. A percentage tells us how large that problem is relative to the size of the dataset.

One missing value in a ten-row dataset means ten percent of the data in that column is missing. One missing value in a million-row dataset is usually much less important.

[tts-break]

Run the code and look at both the count and percentage. Notice that the code creates a small missingness report and sorts the columns so the most incomplete columns appear first.

This pattern is useful in real projects because it gives you a quick overview of data completeness.

Do not decide what to do with missing values yet. The goal here is only to understand where they are and how serious the problem may be.

slides.title: Decide how to handle missing values
slides.transcript:
There is no single rule for handling every missing value.

Sometimes dropping a row is reasonable. Sometimes filling the value is appropriate. Sometimes the missing value should remain because the missingness itself is meaningful. And sometimes the best decision is to investigate the source of the data before doing anything.

[tts-break]

In the example, we use the median to fill a missing satisfaction score. This is only a teaching example. In a real project, you should first ask whether the median makes sense for that variable and for the analytical purpose.

Be careful with automatic rules such as filling every numeric column with the mean or deleting every row that contains any missing value. Those choices can introduce bias or remove useful information.

The important habit is to connect each cleaning decision to a reason that you can explain.

slides.title: Find duplicate records
slides.transcript:
Duplicates can inflate counts, totals, and averages, but not every repeated value is a duplicate.

You first need to decide what defines a unique observation.

In this dataset, order ID is supposed to identify one order. If the same order ID appears twice with the same information, that may be a true duplicate. But a customer ID could legitimately appear many times because one customer can place many orders.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the rows that share the same order ID before removing anything. This is safer than calling drop duplicates immediately.

The code uses the subset argument to focus on the column that should be unique.

In a real project, you may need several columns together to define uniqueness, such as patient ID plus visit date, or product ID plus transaction ID.

The key idea is to understand the meaning of the identifier before deciding what is duplicated.

slides.title: Convert data types safely
slides.transcript:
Data types matter because Pandas uses them to decide what operations are possible.

A number stored as text cannot be summarized correctly until we convert it. A date stored as a string cannot support reliable date operations until it becomes a datetime value.

In the example, we use to numeric and to datetime with errors set to coerce.

[tts-break]

Coerce means that invalid values are converted to missing values instead of causing the program to stop.

This is useful because conversion becomes part of the quality audit. The invalid date becomes visible as a missing datetime value, and a missing or malformed amount becomes a missing numeric value.

Run the code and compare the values and data types before and after conversion.

Remember that conversion does not automatically solve the problem. It helps us identify which values need further investigation.

slides.title: Clean text categories
slides.transcript:
Text categories often contain small differences that create false groups.

For example, Web, web, and web with extra spaces may all represent the same channel. If we do not standardize them, Pandas will treat them as separate categories.

The example uses string methods to remove extra spaces and standardize capitalization.

[tts-break]

Run the code and compare the value counts after cleaning. This is a useful validation step because it confirms that categories were combined the way you intended.

In real datasets, you may also need to fix spelling differences or map several labels into one standard category.

For example, North Carolina, NC, and N.C. may all need to become one value.

The goal is not to make text look nicer. The goal is to make categories represent the same concept consistently.

slides.title: Validate ranges and business rules
slides.transcript:
A value can have the correct data type and still be wrong.

For example, negative twenty is a valid number in Python. But if the variable represents a purchase amount, a negative value may violate a business rule. A satisfaction score of nine is also numeric, but it is invalid if the allowed scale is one through five.

[tts-break]

This is why domain knowledge matters.

Run the code and notice that we create Boolean conditions to flag invalid values rather than deleting them automatically.

That is an important workflow. First detect the problem, then inspect the affected rows, and only then decide what action is appropriate.

Business rules are often more useful than generic statistical rules because they reflect what the data is supposed to mean.

Always ask whether a value is possible in the real process that generated the data.

slides.title: Outliers are questions, not automatic deletions
slides.transcript:
An outlier is an observation that looks unusual compared with the rest of the data.

It may be an error, but it may also be a legitimate and important case.

For example, a very large order could be a misplaced decimal point, a wholesale customer, or a real high-value transaction. Those possibilities require different actions.

[tts-break]

This is why I want you to think of outliers as questions rather than automatic deletions.

A useful workflow is detect, investigate, then decide.

You may keep the value, correct it using a trusted source, transform the variable, analyze it separately, or exclude it when you have a defensible reason.

Simply writing “I removed all outliers” is not enough.

In a professional analysis, you should explain how the unusual values were identified and why the chosen treatment makes sense.

slides.title: Flag outliers with the IQR rule
slides.transcript:
The interquartile range, or IQR, is one simple statistical method for flagging unusually high or low values.

First, we calculate Q1, the twenty-fifth percentile, and Q3, the seventy-fifth percentile. The IQR is Q3 minus Q1.

Then we create lower and upper fences using one point five times the IQR.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the values that fall outside those fences.

The important word here is flagged. The IQR rule does not prove that a value is incorrect. It tells us that the value is unusual relative to the middle part of the distribution.

This method is useful for screening, but context still matters.

If the flagged value is eleven hundred, the next step might be checking the source record or understanding whether a different type of customer generated that order.

slides.title: Explore categorical variables
slides.transcript:
For categorical variables, a good starting point is frequency.

Value counts tell us how many observations belong to each category. Normalized value counts convert those counts into proportions or percentages.

Run the code and inspect the channel distribution.

[tts-break]

Ask whether one category dominates the data, whether any categories are unexpectedly rare, and whether missing values are still present.

These simple summaries can reveal important information before we create charts or statistical models.

For example, if ninety-five percent of transactions come from one channel, later comparisons across channels may be unstable because the smaller groups contain very few observations.

Categorical EDA is not complicated, but it gives you important context about the structure and balance of the dataset.

slides.title: Explore numeric variables
slides.transcript:
Numeric EDA helps us understand the center, spread, and range of a variable.

The describe function gives us several useful statistics at once, including count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles, and maximum.

In the example, pay special attention to the mean and median.

[tts-break]

If the mean is much larger than the median, that can be a clue that the distribution is right-skewed or contains an extreme high value.

The maximum can also help us notice unusual observations.

Do not treat these statistics as conclusions by themselves. They are clues that guide the next question.

For example, if the maximum is much larger than the seventy-fifth percentile, you may want to look at the distribution or inspect that specific record more carefully.

slides.title: Compare groups during EDA
slides.transcript:
Overall summaries can hide differences between groups.

For example, the overall average order amount may look reasonable, but one region may have much higher values than the others.

Grouped EDA helps us compare categories such as regions, departments, channels, or customer segments.

[tts-break]

Run the code and compare count, median, mean, and maximum for each region.

The count matters because a group with only one or two observations should be interpreted cautiously.

Also notice the difference between mean and median within each group. If one group has an extreme value, the mean may move much more than the median.

At this stage, treat group differences as patterns to investigate. A difference in a summary table does not automatically mean the groups are statistically different in the larger population.

slides.title: Document your cleaning decisions
slides.transcript:
A clean Data frame is useful, but a reproducible cleaning process is much more valuable.

You should be able to explain what issue you found, what action you took, how many values were affected, and why the decision was reasonable.

The example on the slide shows a simple cleaning log.

[tts-break]

Imagine that another analyst receives your dataset six months later. They should not have to guess why Web and web became the same category or why certain rows disappeared.

In real projects, keep cleaning steps in code rather than manually editing the original file.

A notebook, script, or pipeline creates an audit trail that can be rerun when new data arrives.

Good documentation also protects you from your own memory. If you return to the project later, the code and notes explain exactly what was changed and why.

slides.title: Mini cleaning pipeline
slides.transcript:
Now we combine several cleaning decisions into one workflow.

The example removes a confirmed duplicate, converts amount and date safely, standardizes region and channel labels, and creates flags for invalid numeric values.

Read the code from top to bottom and connect each line to a specific data-quality problem.

[tts-break]

Notice that the pipeline does not silently delete every suspicious row.

Invalid amounts and scores are flagged so they remain visible for review.

This is a strong pattern for real analytical work: automate what you know is safe, preserve uncertainty where investigation is still needed, and keep the transformations readable.

Run the code and inspect both the cleaned Data frame and the missing-value summary after conversion.

A good pipeline should make the data better while also making the cleaning logic easy to understand.

slides.title: Check the data after cleaning
slides.transcript:
Cleaning does not end when the code finishes running.

You need to verify that the result actually matches the rules you intended to apply.

Recheck duplicates. Recount missing values. Inspect the data types. Look at category values. Count rule violations. Compare the number of rows before and after cleaning.

[tts-break]

The code on this slide demonstrates simple quality checks.

In larger projects, these checks can become functions or automated tests.

For example, you might assert that order IDs are unique, that amount is never negative, or that satisfaction values stay between one and five.

The important idea is that successful execution is not proof of correctness.

A program can run perfectly and still produce a logically wrong dataset.

Always validate the result after cleaning.

slides.title: Practice challenge
slides.transcript:
Now you will build the cleaning and EDA workflow yourself.

Start with the provided messy dataset. First audit it. Then remove the confirmed duplicate, convert date and amount safely, standardize region and channel labels, and flag invalid values.

After that, create a missing-value report and summarize amount by region.

[tts-break]

Do not try to write the entire solution at once.

Complete one step, run it, inspect the result, and then continue.

That approach makes debugging easier and helps you understand what each transformation changes.

At the end, write two or three sentences about what you found during EDA.

The goal is not only to produce a cleaned table. The goal is to explain the quality problems, the decisions you made, and the patterns you observed after cleaning.

slides.title: Module 12 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
Module 12 focused on one central idea: trust the data before you trust the result.

You learned how to audit a dataset, measure missingness, handle duplicates, convert types safely, standardize categories, apply domain rules, investigate outliers, and validate the result after cleaning.

You also used simple EDA to examine categorical and numeric variables and compare groups.

[tts-break]

These skills are foundational because every later analytical method depends on the quality of the input.

In Module 13, we will build directly on this work. We will use descriptive statistics and visualization to study distributions, compare groups, and examine relationships more clearly.

When you move to the next module, keep the same habit: do not calculate a statistic or create a chart until you understand what the underlying data represents.
